title: Two-mask array: hole-and-slit concentric annular 3D DRAM cells
idea: Limit: the whole array may use only two critical masks. One hole mask through 96 Si/SiGe tiers defines vertical bitlines, and a timed lateral recess from each hole carves a concentric ring per tier (BL core, then an annular channel gated by the tier plates above and below, then an outer ring capacitor). One slit mask cuts the plates into wordline regions, so a cell is the crossing of one hole and one tier-region.
why: Facts 2 and 4: about 10,000 nm2 per tier-cell at 100 nm hole pitch gives about 104 nm2/bit over 96 tiers (8x denser than 6F2 at 12 nm) with zero EUV array layers.

title: In-stack voltage-window decoder replaces wordline staircase
idea: Limit: zero staircase area. Each tier is grown with in-situ graded doping so its select device has a distinct threshold. Two series select gates in the same film, one inversion-mode and one junctionless depletion-mode, open a voltage window that turns on exactly one tier. So two vertical gate electrodes address 64+ tiers with no stair contacts.
why: Fact 7 and 3D cost: staircase plus contacts can take 10-20% of a 3D die and grows with tier count; this makes tier addressing O(1) area.

title: Janus pillar: bitline at the waist, cells at both ends
idea: Limit: capacitor height capped at 300 nm per side. A 4F2 vertical pillar has a buried bitline contacting its middle. The upper half has its own gate and frontside capacitor. After wafer flip and bond, the lower half gets a second gate and a backside capacitor, so the pillar holds two independent cells.
why: Facts 1 and 4: 2F2 per bit with two short, low-AR capacitors instead of one 75:1 pillar, about 3x density at the same F.

title: Tier-multiplexed sense-amp layer shared by sixteen bonded array layers
idea: Limit: 0% periphery on any array die. Sixteen thin array layers are hybrid-bonded onto one bottom sense-amp layer. Each layer's bitline group reaches the sense amps through a per-layer select transistor in a vertical bond-via column, so one sense-amp row serves 16 layers in turn.
why: Fact 7: periphery is about 49% of the die; amortizing sense amps over 16 layers cuts periphery per bit about 16x and lifts array efficiency toward 90%.

title: 64-cell vertical bitlines let 1.5 fF capacitors suffice
idea: Limit: Cs may not exceed 1.5 fF. Make every bitline vertical and only as long as the tier count (64 cells, about 2 um), so bitline capacitance falls to about 3 fF versus about 50-80 fF planar. The transfer ratio Cs/(Cs+Cb) jumps about 5x, and a lateral capacitor that fits inside a tier gives enough signal.
why: Facts 1 and 2: breaks the 4.5-5.4 fF requirement that blocks 3D lateral capacitors and keeps about 150 mV of read signal.

title: Micro-mat 3D array with 64-byte pages via bonded local drivers
idea: Limit: a page may not exceed 64 bytes. Cut wordlines into 512-bit segments, each driven by its own local wordline driver placed on a hybrid-bonded logic layer directly beneath that mat, so the extra drivers cost no array area.
why: Fact 8: removing 128x overfetch takes random-access energy from about 5.9 pJ per useful bit toward about 1 pJ.

title: One crucible wafer seeds twenty monocrystalline tiers by donor reuse
idea: Limit: at most one CZ (quartz-crucible) wafer per 20 tiers. Smart-cut transfers 60 nm single-crystal Si films from one donor onto the stack one tier at a time, with refinishing CMP between transfers. The donor is reused about 20 times before it is sliced into test wafers.
why: Resource chokepoint: Spruce Pine high-purity quartz; cuts crucible-grown Si per tier-bit about 20x while keeping crystalline access transistors.

title: Stack-sidewall lithography replaces TSVs in memory stacks
idea: Limit: zero TSVs. Stack dies flush, polish the stack edge, and pattern a redistribution layer directly on the stack sidewall with laser direct imaging. Each die's edge pads join vertical sidewall buses.
why: Fact 6: removes the TSV keep-out and yield tax (about 3x area per bit and 20-30% yield loss for HBM) for stacks of 12-24 dies.

title: Stack-of-stacks: hybrid-bonded sixteen-tier superlattice modules
idea: Limit: strain allows no more than 20 Si/SiGe pairs per epi run. Grow strain-safe 16-tier modules on separate wafers, process their lateral cells, then hybrid-bond eight modules face-to-face and back-to-back with vertical bitline vias crossing each bond.
why: Fact 2: reaches 128 tiers without epi relaxation defects, and module yield is binned before stacking.

title: Mirror-tier pairs share one horizontal bitline sheet
idea: Limit: half a metal layer per tier. Build tiers as mirrored pairs around a single horizontal bitline plane, with cells above and below contacting the same bitline. This halves bitline layers and cuts tier pitch about 25%.
why: Fact 2: more tiers per micron of stack height and fewer deposition/etch layers per bit, about 1.3x density per stack height.

title: Vertical charge-coupled shift columns with zero transistors per bit
idea: Limit: no access transistor per bit. Each 4F2 column is a stack of 3-phase clocked gate tiers forming CCD potential wells. Charge packets shift down the column at about 2 GHz to one sense node at its base, giving page access in about 10-30 ns.
why: Facts 1-3: about 20 bits per 4F2 footprint with no capacitor or transistor per bit; endurance is unlimited because the storage is charge.

title: Maskless three-beam interference lithography for hexagonal cell arrays
idea: Limit: no photomask for the array. Expose the whole cell field with three-beam laser interference, which prints a perfect hexagonal pillar lattice in one shot. Periphery is defined separately by cheap i-line or ArF litho and stitched at mat edges.
why: Fact 4: replaces several EUV array layers with a tool costing about 1/50 as much, and hex packing gains about 15% over square.

title: Grounded shield-plate tiers that make row hammer impossible
idea: Limit: no row may have an electrically coupled neighbor. Insert a thin grounded metal plane between every pair of cell tiers, and alternate wordline tiers between different banks. The plane blocks both capacitive crosstalk and carrier migration from aggressor rows.
why: Fact 9: pushes the flip threshold from about 1k activations to far beyond any refresh window and removes mitigation logic and its bandwidth cost.

title: Voltage-stacked tiers recycle bitline charge in series
idea: Limit: supply current cut 8x. Run eight tier groups in series between 8 V and 0 V, each swinging only its own 1 V slice. Charge dumped by one tier's bitline precharge becomes the supply of the tier below.
why: Fact 10: breaks the CV2 voltage floor at system level; up to about 2-4x lower array energy and 8x less power-delivery current and bump count.

title: Bookshelf memory: upright thin dies edge-bonded onto logic
idea: Limit: fixed footprint, no TSVs, and more than 32 dies. Stand 20 um thin DRAM dies on edge like books across the logic die, and hybrid-bond their polished edge pads directly to the logic surface. About 50 dies per mm of row.
why: Facts 5 and 6: far more dies per footprint than horizontal HBM stacks, a TSV-free signal path, and each die cools through its faces.

title: Spare-tier redundancy with per-column remap fuses in bonded logic
idea: Limit: a 128-tier stack must still yield at least 95%. Build 136 tiers, test each column, and map up to eight defective tiers per column to spares through a remap table held in the bonded logic layer, replacing classic row/column sparing.
why: Fact 2: turns compound tier yield (0.995^128 = 53%) into high stack yield, making high tier counts economic.

title: Wafer-scale stitched DRAM plane bonded to wafer-scale compute
idea: Limit: no reticle boundary and no dicing. Stitch array tiles across a full 300 mm wafer with redundant tile routing, then hybrid-bond the whole memory wafer face-to-face onto a wafer-scale compute wafer.
why: Facts 5 and 6: tens of PB/s of vertical bandwidth at sub-0.5 pJ/bit with no package, interposer or TSV overhead.

title: GPU-owned sense amps: array stack bonded straight onto accelerator
idea: Limit: no base die and no DRAM-process periphery. Array-only layers with 8:1 bitline muxes are hybrid-bonded at fine pitch directly onto the accelerator die. Sense amps, decoders and controllers are built in the accelerator's 3 nm logic, at about 1/4 the area of DRAM-process periphery.
why: Facts 5 and 7: removes the HBM PHY and base die; data movement drops toward 0.3 pJ/bit and array dies become near-100% cells.

title: In-plane side-gated tiers: wordline silicided from the tier itself
idea: Limit: zero tungsten. Next to each tier's lateral channel, a parallel strip of the same Si tier, across a narrow ALD-dielectric-filled slit, is converted to NiSi and becomes an in-plane side-gate wordline. No metal fill goes into deep recesses.
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China about 80%) and Fact 2: removes W replacement-gate fill and its void and stress problems in high-tier stacks.

title: Open tier-PDK and known-good-tier marketplace
idea: Limit: no single company may own the whole stack. Publish an open interface spec for bondable array tiers (pad pitch, test pads, select-switch protocol) so fabs of many sizes sell tested array tiers to independent stackers that assemble them on logic.
why: Capital intensity: splits a $15B monolithic fab into smaller tier fabs and stackers, so capacity scales in about $1-2B increments.

title: Backside bitlines buried under a 4F2 vertical-channel array
idea: Limit: the front side may carry only capacitors and wordlines. After the 4F2 pillars are formed, flip-bond the wafer, thin it, and pattern bitlines on the exposed pillar bottoms from the backside. This removes bitline contacts and buried-bitline doping steps from the front.
why: Fact 4: true 4F2 (vs 6F2, about 1.5x density) with fewer front-side critical layers and lower bitline resistance.

title: Cross-shaped four-way cells around every vertical bitline
idea: Limit: vertical bitline holes cannot get denser. Slice each tier around a vertical bitline into four quadrant channels, so one bitline serves four lateral cells per tier instead of two.
why: Facts 2 and 7: halves vertical bitlines and sense-amp connections per bit, about 1.4x tier density.

title: Stack-only U.S. fab: domestic 3D integration of imported array wafers
idea: Limit: no new DRAM front-end fab for three years. Fund U.S. hybrid-bonding and tier-stacking lines that buy array and periphery wafers from several allied sources and do all 3D integration, test and redundancy remap domestically.
why: U.S. manufacturability (about 1-2% share): captures the highest-value 3D step in 18-24 months at a fraction of front-end capital.

title: Interposer-as-memory: oxide DRAM tiers in the passive interposer
idea: Under 400 C, build four oxide-channel 1T1C DRAM tiers in the BEOL of the large passive silicon interposer that already sits under the GPU and HBM, patterned with ArF at 40 nm. The interposer becomes about 100 GB of near memory directly under the compute die.
why: Facts 5 and 6: about 150 Mb per mm2 per tier on about 2500 mm2 of otherwise idle silicon, sub-pJ/bit access, no TSVs and no extra wafer.

title: Display-fab DRAM: oxide memory tiles on Gen-8.5 glass panels
idea: Under 400 C, display IGZO lines (all at or below 350 C) pattern stacked oxide 1T1C arrays on 2.2x2.5 m glass at about 1.5 um rules, using thick-film capacitors. Panels are diced into memory tiles that are bonded under logic as capacity tiers.
why: Capital intensity and cost per bit: about 25x the area of a 300 mm wafer per substrate, on depreciated tools; good for bulk capacity tiers.

title: Coarse-litho tall stack: 48 ArF-dry tiers beat EUV density
idea: Because nothing exceeds 400 C, oxide 4F2 cross-point tiers can be stacked sequentially without disturbing lower tiers. Each tier uses only two ArF-dry masks at 65 nm, and density comes from tier count instead of litho.
why: Fact 4: 48 tiers at 65 nm 4F2 give about 350 nm2/bit (2.5x denser than 6F2 at 12 nm) with zero EUV; capital moves to cheap litho.

title: Registration-free anodic alumina capacitor forest at room temperature
idea: Under 400 C, anodize a sputtered 3 um Al film over the transistor tier at room temperature to self-form 25 nm pores (AR over 100) with no litho or plasma etch. Each storage-node pad is wider than the pore pitch, so it captures 2-3 pores. ALD TiN/ZrO2/TiN at 300 C lines the pores.
why: Facts 1 and 4: AR over 100 without a high-AR etch tool; Cs above 6 fF with no capacitor mask.

title: Capacitor-first substrate: MacEtch forest with the wafer as plate
idea: Under 400 C, metal-assisted chemical etching (Au mesh in HF/H2O2 at room temperature) drills 20 nm holes at AR about 150 into a doped Si wafer. After an ALD MIM liner at 300 C, the oxide transistor tier is built on top, and the bulk wafer itself is the common cell plate.
why: Fact 1: breaks the 60-75:1 etch limit with a wet bench instead of a $10M+ etcher; Cs 8-10 fF.

title: Rutile TiO2 grown on the ruthenium bitline template
idea: Under 400 C, the Ru electrode lines of each tier are surface-oxidized to RuO2, which templates rutile Al-doped TiO2 by ALD at 280 C with k of about 80-100. These are planar or shallow-trench capacitors integrated straight onto the electrode tier.
why: Fact 1: reaches the k of about 70 the brief says is needed, so 5 fF fits at about 25:1 AR instead of 75:1.

title: Spatial-ALD nanolaminate replaces Si/SiGe epitaxy for 128 tiers
idea: Under 400 C, deposit 128 alternating 8 nm IGZO (or indium-free ZTO) channel layers and 20 nm AlOx sacrificial layers in one spatial-ALD run, then build lateral 3D DRAM cells by hole/slit recess as in Si/SiGe flows.
why: Fact 2: removes about $5M epi tools and strain limits; tier deposition cost per wafer about 1/5 and tier count is not limited by strain.

title: Monolayer MoS2 tiers at 15 nm pitch: 256 tiers per 4 um
idea: Under 400 C, wafer-scale MOCVD grows monolayer MoS2 (0.7 nm channel) for each tier. With an ALD gate stack, each tier is about 15 nm thick, and the atomic-thin body plus 1.8 eV gap gives aA-level leakage.
why: Facts 2 and 3: about 3x more tiers per stack height than Si tiers (about 45 nm), and refresh intervals stretch from 64 ms toward minutes.

title: Junctionless transferred-silicon tiers from pre-doped donor wafers
idea: Under 400 C, H/He co-implant splits a heavily pre-doped donor at 350 C after a 250 C plasma-activated bond. The 10 nm single-crystal film becomes junctionless access transistors that never need a dopant-activation anneal.
why: Fact 2: crystalline-Si mobility and controlled leakage in 3D tiers without the 1000 C steps that stop monolithic stacking.

title: Copper wordlines and bitlines buried beneath the cell array
idea: Under 400 C, an oxide 4F2 vertical-channel array never heats buried wiring past 400 C, so buried word and bitlines can be damascene Cu, normally banned under a DRAM cell flow. Sub-array lines get about 2-3x longer per local driver.
why: Fact 7: fewer sub-wordline drivers and sense-amp stripes; about 10-15% die area goes back to cells.

title: Sacrificial-polymer air-gap bitlines halve bitline capacitance
idea: Under 400 C, fill between bitlines with a polynorbornene-type sacrificial polymer, cap it with porous ALD SiO2, and decompose it through the cap at 350 C to leave air gaps. This works only because no later step needs high temperature.
why: Facts 1 and 10: about 35-45% lower Cb, so Cs can drop by the same fraction or bitline voltage swing can fall.

title: Ga2O3-channel tiers with planar 0.5 fF capacitors
idea: Under 400 C, ALD amorphous Ga2O3 (4.8 eV gap) access transistors leak orders of magnitude less than Si. Each tier then needs only a flat 0.5 fF MIM capacitor beside the transistor, with no pillar at all, and tiers become simple planar layers.
why: Facts 1 and 3: retention long enough for a 0.5 fF node removes the high-AR capacitor and nearly eliminates refresh energy.

title: Oxide-CMOS sense amplifiers distributed inside every tier
idea: Under 400 C, each tier carries its own tiny sense-amp strip of n-IGZO and p-SnO transistors deposited at 250 C, sensing short local bitlines. The bonded base logic only handles global I/O.
why: Fact 7 and 3D scaling: periphery stops growing with tier count; local sensing tolerates small Cs.

title: Hexagonal block-copolymer holes for vertical oxide-channel rings
idea: Under 400 C, cylinder-forming block copolymer annealed at 250 C self-assembles a 28 nm-pitch hexagonal hole lattice. Each hole gets an ALD ring channel and gate-all-around wordline, giving an EUV-free vertical cell array.
why: Fact 4: sub-30 nm pitch with no EUV and about 15% hex-packing gain; cell masks drop from 5-7 EUV to 1 ArF guide pattern.

title: Area-selective ALD grows tier-to-tier vias bottom-up
idea: Under 400 C, Ru grows by area-selective ALD only on exposed Ru landing pads, not on the surrounding dielectric, at 300 C. Each new tier's contacts self-align upward with no via lithography.
why: Fact 4: removes one critical mask per tier in monolithic stacks, about 30% fewer litho steps over 32 tiers.

title: Room-temperature surface-activated bonding of 5 um memory dies
idea: Under 400 C, Ar-beam surface activation bonds Cu/SiO2 die faces at room temperature, so thermal-expansion warpage never builds up. This allows 5 um dies and 32-48-high stacks.
why: Fact 6: about 3x bits per stack height with no thermocompression yield loss.

title: Known-good-tier lamination: binned two-tier oxide modules
idea: Under 400 C, fabricate two-tier oxide DRAM modules on cheap glass carriers, test and bin each one, then laminate only good modules by 250 C Cu-Cu hybrid bonding into 16-tier stacks. Modules are made in parallel, not in series.
why: Fact 2 and capital intensity: decouples stack yield from tier count and cuts cycle time about 8x versus sequential tier processing.

title: Redox-molecule pseudocapacitor storage node on nanoporous electrode
idea: Under 400 C, a nanoporous Ru storage node (about 50x surface area) is coated at 200 C with a monolayer of thermally robust porphyrin redox molecules. Bits are stored as molecular oxidation state, so many electrons are packed per nm2 at low voltage.
why: Facts 1 and 10: about 10x charge per footprint versus dielectric capacitors at about 0.5 V reads; planar storage nodes.

title: Backside-BEOL DRAM on backside-power logic wafers
idea: Under 400 C, in the backside metal stack that backside-power-delivery logic processes already build, insert two to four oxide 1T1C tiers between power rails, directly under the logic transistors and about 1 um away.
why: Fact 5: GB-class memory at about 0.1 pJ/bit with no added wafer, package or bonding step.

title: Tungsten-free plated copper staircases with self-forming barriers
idea: Under 400 C, fill all staircase contacts and vertical straps by room-temperature electroplated CuMn. A 300 C anneal self-forms a 2 nm MnSiOx barrier, so no W CVD is used anywhere in the 3D array.
why: Tungsten chokepoint: removes W from 3D wiring with about 3x lower contact resistance for tall stacks.

title: MLCC-in-a-cell: forty-plate interdigitated capacitor per bit
idea: Under 400 C, ALD forty alternating Ru and TiN plates separated by 4 nm ZrO2 (crystalline as deposited at about 275 C). Selectively recess Ru on one hole sidewall and TiN on the other so each cell's two contacts tie to alternating plates, like an MLCC termination.
why: Fact 1: about 5 fF in a 40x40 nm footprint at about 9:1 AR instead of 75:1; the capacitor scales by plate count, not etch depth.

title: One nanoimprint template patterns all thirty-two identical tiers
idea: Under 400 C, room-temperature nanoimprint lithography patterns every oxide tier at 14 nm half-pitch with a single master template, because all tiers are identical. A self-aligned crossed-line imprint relaxes overlay.
why: Fact 4: tool capex about 1/4 of EUV, and template cost is spread over 32 tiers.

title: Packaging houses become DRAM fabs using 400 C tool sets
idea: Under 400 C, advanced-packaging and OSAT plants already run PVD, plating, ALD, steppers and hybrid bonders. They add oxide DRAM tier modules on purchased CMOS periphery wafers, with no furnaces or EUV.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: about 1/5 the capex per wafer start and uses existing U.S. packaging sites in 12-18 months.
